paras: The lynching of Lee Hall took place early on February 7, 1903, when a mob took Hall, a Black man accused of shooting Sheriff D. A. Crawford, from the jail at Wrightsville, Johnson County, Georgia, and hanged and shot him. A coroner's jury attributed his death to "unknown persons," and the sheriff died of his wound four days later. Many white papers carried the story, some reporting that the mob took Hall's ears and fingers as souvenirs; Black weeklies printed brief notices and later counted him among the year's lynching victims.

According to the Savannah Morning News, Crawford left Wrightsville on the afternoon of Wednesday, February 4, with a warrant for Hall, who was charged with gambling. At Claude Joiner's store, about 12 miles out, the paper reported, Hall rushed outside and shot the sheriff through the right lung.

A posse that included Joiner captured Hall on the morning of February 6 and that evening turned him over to Coroner T. L. Parris, who was acting as jailer. Crowds arrived after dark, and an Associated Press dispatch said threats made early in the night later "somewhat subsided." About midnight, the Savannah correspondent wrote, a "well organized" mob battered in the jail door with a large timber and broke open Hall's cell with hammers and crowbars. The AP account said only that the mob "forced the jail officials to deliver Hall."

The mob took Hall, still handcuffed, about a mile out to the edge of Cedar Creek, hanged him from a tree beside the public road, and riddled his body with bullets. Communication with the governor had been cut off, and the authorities were described as "powerless to prevent the lynching."

Crowds viewed the body until it was cut down for an inquest, at which Coroner Harris's jury heard no evidence on the participants and found death from wounds "inflicted by unknown persons." Notices were also left warning Black residents "most active heretofore in politics" to leave the community. No report of arrests, indictments or a trial of anyone in the mob appears in the coverage.
Crawford died on February 11 and was buried in Wrightsville the next day. On April 1 Lewis Davis was elected to succeed him.

The first wire, datelined Dublin, Georgia, ran as two sentences under headlines such as "Lee Hall Lynched" and "Murderer is Lynched." A longer AP dispatch from Wrightsville appeared as "Lynched for Wounding a Sheriff" and "Negro Lynched While His Victim Yet Lives."

The Savannah Morning News headlined its account "WAS SHOT TO PIECES," called Hall a "negro desperado," and in April wrote that he had "paid the penalty at the hands of 'Judge Lynch.'" The New York Sun instead led with the mutilation, "Horrible Souvenirs Taken by Georgia Lynchers," as did an Iowa paper.

Black papers carried little of their own on the case. On February 14 the Baltimore Afro-American reprinted the AP text as "Taken From Jail and Lynched," and the Richmond Planet gave it one sentence; neither added comment. Later Black-press tallies listed him: the Wichita Searchlight and Sedalia Times under February 7 for "murder," and the Seattle Republican as "Lee Hale" under "Mobocracy's Bloody Reign." The Chicago Broad Ax dated the lynching February 4, and a white-press "Mob Law" list gave "Negro hanged, Wrightsville, Ga., February 8."

Accounts differ on how Hall was killed. The local Savannah report described a hanging and shooting with no mutilation, while the Sun's Augusta dispatch said Hall was tied half a mile from the jail, his throat cut, over a hundred shots fired into him, and his ears and fingers taken. The AP put the place "a few miles" from Wrightsville.

Only the Sun gave the mob's size, "over three hundred men," and it placed the shooting in Washington County, where the other reports placed it in Johnson County. The Savannah paper also later dated the shooting "Feb. 1," against the Wednesday of its first report.

Most papers ran the Dublin or AP wire under headlines such as 'Murderer is Lynched', 'Lynched for Wounding a Sheriff' and 'Negro Lynched While His Victim Yet Lives'.
The Sun headlined the mutilation as 'Horrible Souvenirs Taken by Georgia Lynchers'; an Iowa paper ran 'Negro Fingers for Souvenirs'.
The Afro-American printed the AP text as 'Taken From Jail and Lynched' and the Richmond Planet a one-sentence item, both without comment.
Later tallies placed Hall among the year's victims, the Seattle Republican under 'Mobocracy's Bloody Reign' and the Wichita Searchlight citing deaths 'by lawless men'.
